utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have a third point to address, and that has to do with the observations of the Prosecution regarding the oral motion of the defence. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor. Submissions by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I turn to that issue, if I might, there is one additional issue that I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to, and also seek the Trial Chamber's leave. On the 8th of November, as the Chamber is aware, the Defence filed a motion in which they sought to preclude the Prosecution from cross-examining with respect to the presence of the Croatian army, and in the same motion, they requested that the Prosecution not make reference or use the terms "detain" or "detention." On the 10th of November, the Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecution to respond to that motion within 15 days. As I was finalising the Prosecution response to that motion last evening, it occurred road to me that the 15 days perhaps referred to the filing date of the Defence motion rather than the time when the Trial Chamber informed us that we had 15 days. As a result of that, Mr. President, I, first thing this morning, attempted to contact the Chamber's legal officer, the one who's normally present with us but who I see is not here today. At the same time, I directed my case manager to file our response today. And I raise this issue, Mr. President, in the event that the 15 days commenced from the Defence filing, clearly we missed the deadline, which would have been yesterday. And so we are at this point seeking your leave to accept that filing as if it had been filed in time, again, assuming that the 15-day period commenced on the 8th when the Defence filed rather than the 10th, when the Chamber informed us that we had 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in our view, the 15 days ran from the moment when we granted you 15 days, that is, starting from the 10th. So the 15 days do not run from the moment when the motion was filed but from the moment when we informed you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, in which case what I said is just moot. We filed our response earlier this morning, and it should be available from the Registry today at some point, I hope. Let me turn, then, Mr. President and Your Honours, to the issue that was raised on the 9th of November, and the Prosecution is grateful for this opportunity to respond. There are several issues involved, and the Prosecution will briefly respond to these issues after making a few general comments about what we would submit is the proper scope of cross-examination. At the outset, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution asserts that the scope of cross-examination is wide, as reflected in the provisions of Rule 90(H), which requires the cross-examining party to put their case to a witness when a witness is able to give evidence that is relevant to the subject matter of the case. Once a link has been established between the knowledge of such a witness and certain documents, in our respectful submission, the cross-examining party should be permitted to put the contents of documents to a witness. In some cases, it might be helpful to the Trial Chamber to have the document in question admitted into evidence, while in other situations, this may not be necessary; all that may be needed is to confront the witness with the document or documents in question. Also, as a general rule, in our submission, where the document is used to test the credibility of a witness, there is no legal requirement for a foundation to be laid with respect to the document that is used to test the witness' credibility. Rather, the cross-examining party must lay a foundation in the form of questions put to the witness in order to put the issue of credibility into play. It's important, Mr. President and Your Honours, to keep in mind that when the Prosecution was putting together its exhibit list, it was not possible for us to anticipate the witnesses that the Defence might call in its case. And consequently, and in light of the large number of documents which the Prosecution possesses, our view is it should not be a surprise that the Prosecution possesses documents which were not disclosed because they didn't fall within the regular disclosure regime, or which were not on the Prosecution exhibit list. Some of these documents may, in our submission, however, now be shown to Defence witnesses who appear before this Tribunal to testify. At the same time, and along the same lines, because the identity of the Defence witnesses was obviously not known to the Prosecution before or during the Prosecution case, and because many of these witnesses testified about all sorts of events and incidents in their evidence in chief, the Prosecution would submit, as I'll be discussing in a few minutes, our position is that we should be allowed broad latitude in terms of cross-examining witnesses with documents and, if need be or if it's helpful to the Chamber, tendering such documents into evidence. We believe that the usual criteria which governs cross-examination, including relevance, perhaps prior inconsistent statements of the witness, or the credibility of the witness, in these cases, we should be allowed to use documents which we had not previously disclosed since they did not fall within Rule 68 or on our exhibit list. The Prosecution submits that this is particularly true in the present case, since the Defence have been permitted to introduce a defence based on the widest possible use of contextual evidence. Because the Trial Chamber that let the Defence lead evidence concerning the military, political, historical, and socio-economic context in which the armed conflict and the alleged crimes occurred, the Prosecution should be permitted to challenge such evidence through cross-examination. However, because our exhibit list and disclosure was premised on the charges and counts in the indictment, and not in anticipation of having to rebut actions taken by the HVO or, for example, crimes committed by the HVO, it was not foreseeable that such material should have been disclosed and placed on our exhibit list. The Prosecution position, Mr. President and Your Honours, is that we could not have anticipated that the Defence would have been permitted to lead evidence on the scope of the entire conflict in the Lasva and Bila River Valleys in 1993, since our indictment focussed on discrete incidents in that conflict. The Defence have argued that the proper time for the Prosecution to adduce such evidence is through a rebuttal case and not through the Defence case, through Defence witnesses. While the Prosecution appreciates this position, it raises problems, in our respectful view. For example, the Prosecution could be faced in rebuttal with several choices in order to get these documents before the Trial Chamber. First, we would seek to tender them from the bar table in a case in rebuttal, as was done during the Prosecution case in chief, over strenuous objections of the Defence. Second, we could recall or seek leave to recall the relevant witnesses, many of whom would be Defence witnesses, to speak about the documents that would be in our possession. In our respectful submission, Mr. President, neither of these ways of proceeding are sound and could result in wasting precious resources and time, especially if the witness' subsequent re-examination consists of only a handful of questions relating to a document or documents. The better course, in our view, would be for the Prosecution to be allowed to show such documents to the Defence witnesses while they're here and to ask them to comment on them. Let me turn to a couple of the specific issues, other issues, raised by the Defence, the first concerning disclosure. As everyone in and around this courtroom is aware, Rule 65 ter (E)(3)(iii) requires the Prosecution to list and disclose the exhibits it tends to -- intends to use or would like to use in its case in chief. Rule 66 governs disclosure of confirmation material, permits the Defence to inspect material within the Prosecution's possession. Rule 68, of course, governs exculpatory and other material. There is no specific rule that governs the disclosure of material for purposes of cross-examination. As this Chamber is aware, the investigation mandate of this Tribunal runs through the end of 2004, and the Prosecution is continuing to investigate alleged crimes relating to other potential suspects. During the course of such investigations, which are not linked to the present case, the OTP occasionally seizes or otherwise takes custody of material and documents which might be relevant in these proceedings, which, in our respectful view, can be an explanation as to why material comes into our possession or has come into our possession both after the commencement of this case and during the course of this case. As the Prosecution reviews this material, we, of course, disclose any and all material that falls within the scope of Rule 68, which is, of course, an ongoing obligation. The Trial Chamber specifically asked the Prosecution to address you on the issue of the general circumstances concerning "the Prosecution's knowledge of the documents that they had or obtained after Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the presentation of its case." Now, Mr. President and Your Honours will recall that Mr. Withopf briefly explained, during the lengthy arguments concerning the admissability of documents tendered by the Prosecution from the bar table during the course of the Prosecution case in chief. Most, but not all, most of the documents which have been tendered into evidence in this case have originated in one of about 10 different document collections. The disclosure of this material is contained in what we refer to as our disclosure log. The disclosure log in this case runs to more than 200 pages of a spreadsheet, and it lists the date on which each individual document, or collection of documents, was disclosed. I thought it might be of some assistance to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence to attempt to summarise what's contained in the disclosure log. I have prepared a chart, a two-page, or page-and-a-half chart which I would ask, with the assistance of the usher, to be distributed to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence. Let me stress, however, that while this is being done, that again, this is only a summary. This document, as I'll explain in a few moments, has certain limitations, as any summary will have. First, let me stress again that there are some documents which do not come from the six or seven or eight collections that are listed here. For the most part, however, with the exception of the documents coming from UNPROFOR and BritBat, which I'll address in just a moment, this chart reflects those collections from which a large majority of the documents used in this case have come. You'll note the second -- the first column indicates the collection name, the name by which the Office of the Prosecutor refers to these collections of documents. Mr. Withopf has used some of these terms earlier in this trial. The second column refers to the ERN range, the internal OTP-assigned number that's unique to each document or each page of each document. These ERN ranges refer to the B/C/S version of the documents for the simple reason that when we go into an archive and either seize or voluntarily take documents, or when a state or an agency provides us with documents, we'll have an entire collection. Those documents will then be sequentially numbered in their original language. When they are submitted for translation, the translations receive a different ERN number reflecting the different version of that document, which is why we've used the original ERN ranges. The third column indicates the date or dates that the documents were obtained by the Prosecution. The fourth column indicates disclosure. Let me emphasise for everyone's benefit that, as a general rule, in this chart, the column indicating disclosure refers to electronic disclosure only for the simple reason that, as I've said, a 200-page spreadsheet containing individual dates, it's simply impossible to capture in any other way other than to say the material was made electronically available, either on CDs or more recently via the electronic disclosure suite. I should also stress that most of those document collections were disclosed in hard-copy format prior to trial, and in some instances, many, many months before trial. The final column addresses a question that Your Honour put to us concerning the method, whether it was a consensual search, whether it was a seizure, whether it was in response to a request from the Office of the Prosecutor to provide documents. We've also indicated whether we have taken copies of the documents or the originals. With this chart, Mr. President, it should be - and Your Honours - it should be possible to identify rough information about most of the documents which have been tendered into evidence or documents which the Prosecution may, in the future, seek to tender, if the Trial Chamber grants us permission to do so. Again, it's a rough summary, and it's an attempt to reduce more than 200 pages down to a page and a half, with the inherent difficulties that that may cause. I think, Mr. President, I have hopefully answered your questions. We do have a couple of other issues that I would like to just address in the context of this discussion. With respect to disclosure of material that might become relevant during the course of the direct examination, either because it's something that was not clearly anticipated by the Prosecution or because it, perhaps, goes to refreshing the witness' recollection or somehow goes to the credibility of the witness, we would assert in those situations and circumstances we should be permitted to show documents to the witness, we should be able to put these documents to the witness, and we should be able to cross-examine the witness on these issues. I would also, before I sit down, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention and the attention of the Defence to a decision in the Kupreskic case, which is case number IT-95-16-T, a decision of the 21st of January, 1999. The decision is titled "Decision on Order of Presentation of Evidence." And I would like to read from pages 3 and 4 of that decision, which relates to the very issue that has arisen in this case. The Trial Chamber in that case stated: "In order to avoid a possible prejudice to an accused which might result from the Prosecution introducing documents in the cross-examination of a witness which the accused had not hitherto had the opportunity to review and to cross-examine the witness upon, the Prosecution must bona fide disclose to the accused at the earliest available opportunity and, at the latest, prior to cross-examination, any new material it wishes to submit to a Defence witness in cross-examination, in order to give the accused due notice." In our respectful submission, Mr. President, this decision stands for two propositions. First, due process and due notice requirements require the Prosecution, at the earliest available opportunity, to disclose material it seeks to tender in cross-examination of Defence witnesses. At the same time, however, this decision, in our respectful view, in light of the language "disclosure, at the latest, prior to cross-examination," simply means that the Defence should not be ambushed with such documents. And as long as the Prosecution discloses such documents prior to cross-examination, our view is that the decision of the Kupreskic Trial Chamber, if adopted by this Trial Chamber, would permit us to do that. Finally, the final issue I would ask to be taken into consideration would be that, in our respectful submission, the interim oral order of the 10th of November, we would ask that that be modified to take into consideration the needs for cross-examining based on documents in terms of refreshing recollection, in terms of potential prior statements, and in terms of the relevance of material which was not foreseeable to the Prosecution prior to trial. We would ask that a balancing test approach be taken similar to the one taken in Kupreskic. The Prosecution would be in the best position to disclose such information as early as possible if we were to get the earliest possible notification from the Defence as to the witnesses coming in the next week. We have indicated on several occasions that we receive our information on our searches based only upon our informing the relevant unit who's coming in the next week or two weeks. I understand the difficulties that the Defence have had in this respect, but it is our respectful view that the more time we have, Mr. President, the more time we will have to review that material and to disclose any potential material that, in our respectful view, we have a duty to seek to put before Your Honours in terms of resolving the ultimate issues involved in this case. With that, Mr. President, again, I thank the Trial Chamber for allowing us some 20 minutes in order to respond to the Defence submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given the Prosecution's submissions, is there anything the Defence would like to say now, or would you prefer to respond at a subsequent date, after having examined the transcript and after having established exactly what your position is. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Judges, good day, Mr. President. Submissions by Mr. Bourgon: Defence counsel will respond to the submissions made by the Prosecution right now. I will try to be as brief as possible. First of all, Mr. President, I'd like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the many comments made by my colleagues that concern disclosure evidence. The Trial Chamber can see, on the basis of the document distributed to everyone in the courtroom, that there's an incredible volume of documents that are included in the new system, what we call the electronic disclosure system or electronic disclosure suite. The volume of material that can be found in this document and in this new system underlies the lack of resources that the Defence counsel has. We don't even have limited access to all these documents included in the electronic system. Mr. President, these documents, this system, have only existed for a very short while, and as the Trial Chamber is well aware, the first time we had access to this system was when we received the documents from the EU Monitoring Mission. However, this is not the subject that the Defence wants to discuss today. As far as the Prosecution's arguments concerning tendering new documents into evidence are concerned, I can summarise them as follows: It wasn't possible for the Prosecution to anticipate the documents that would be used by Defence counsel, nor was it impossible for them to anticipate the witnesses that Defence counsel would be calling. Similarly, the Defence shouldn't be surprised if the Prosecution presents new documents. I think that that's the essence of the Prosecution's arguments. Mr. President, I won't repeat everything I said when I made my submissions the first time, but it's necessary to emphasise the fact that the Prosecution and Defence have diametrically opposed positions in these proceedings. The Defence doesn't bear the burden of proof, but the Prosecution has the burden of proof. They must prove beyond any reasonable doubt all the charges leveled against the accused. Nevertheless, the Prosecution doesn't have any arguments that they need to protect themselves. The purpose of the Prosecution is to present all the elements that they have, and then the accused may raise certain doubts with regard to their guilt. Why? Because it's not permissible to surprise an accused. Justice should not surprise anyone. Either we have proof or we have no proof. Similarly, an accused should have sufficient time to prepare and to assess the impact of new documents presented. The Prosecution adds that there are no rules governing disclosure in the course of its cross-examination. Naturally, Mr. President, it is true that there are no specific rules for the Prosecution or for the Defence as far as the use of any given document is concerned. What the Prosecution failed to mention, however, is that there is a principle, and this principle can be found in Article 21. And these principles are based on the rights of the accused, too. Mr. President, the Prosecution is not playing a game here. The Prosecution is here to present the evidence it has against the accused. The Prosecution has all the means it needs to carry out its investigations. It's been carrying out its investigations since 1993. They can present the evidence against the accused and, above all, a principle has been established, according to which the Prosecution cannot divide its evidence into two parts. They can't say that they'll present sufficient evidence so that we can move to the Defence stage and then say, We'll commence with another stage and introduce new documents, under the pretext that they did not know what the Defence was going to do. This is turning the situation upside down. The Prosecution has its case. They have made certain charges, they have carried out investigations, and they should disclose all their documents. Rule 65 ter (E)(iii) provides for these principles. The Defence should be provided at the same time as the pre-trial brief a list of documents and all the documents. This should enable Defence counsel to prepare its case and to see the witnesses and examine the Prosecution's case. The accused are on this side, not on the other side. Mr. President, once the Prosecution has provided this list, it should include all the evidence they have against an accused. The Prosecution should not keep certain material that they have and say that they don't need it immediately, because they want to wait to see what the Defence is going to say before they examine the documents and decide whether the evidence they have might really be needed, or to see whether it would be sufficient to use only a certain number of documents. Mr. President, when the Defence case commences, there's nothing the Defence has to disclose in terms of information, in terms of knowledge, to the Prosecution. In this system, this is based on the principle that the Prosecution should know everything. The Prosecution shouldn't be surprised by a document, because the Prosecution made the charges, the Prosecution conducted the investigation. So if the Prosecution had a document that they investigated and didn't find, that wouldn't be prejudicial. It would only be prejudicial if they could not present their case. Here before the International Tribunal, we have rules governing the disclosure of evidence, according to which the Defence, before the beginning of its case, provides the Prosecution with all the documents it intends to use. Not just a list of documents but copies of these documents. So the Prosecution knows exactly which issues are going to be raised by the Defence. In certain systems, that would go far beyond what one usually expects from the Defence. But in international proceedings, one believes that this is correct. In order to determine the truth, one should provide the Prosecution with all the documents, and this is what is done. Once the Prosecution has these documents, one should not say that the Prosecution can then use these documents. They should not be allowed to say, Well, now, examine the evidence against the accused that we didn't disclose before, and then decide that this material can be, in fact, used against the accused. As we have already said, the Prosecution may continue to carry out its investigations. This is quite normal, where a new fact is established in a courtroom, and the Prosecution sends investigators into the field to check up on this information. However, to establish new evidence, if they have contrary evidence, according to proceedings before the International Tribunal, this fact can be established, or the Defence's evidence can be challenged in the course of the rebuttal phase. That is when the Prosecution can present new evidence. Finally, Mr. President, as far as cross-examination on the part of the Prosecution is concerned, we believe that there are certain practical issues that the Trial Chamber has to take into consideration, and I welcome the arguments of my colleague who says that it wouldn't be practical to call back a witness in the course of the rebuttal stage; this would result in a waste of time. The Defence, like the Prosecution, is trying to proceed expeditiously. Nevertheless, Mr. President, we believe that any new documents that might be filed by the Prosecution should at least meet the following criteria: Firstly, they should be disclosed to Defence counsel at least 48 hours in advance. Why 48 hours in advance? Because the system is such that, in order to have time to meet the accused, discuss with the accused in their language, and in order to adjust the Defence's strategy, well, this requires a certain amount of time. This is a formal stage. As far as the substance is concerned, Mr. President, the Prosecution should ask the Chamber for leave. Before a witness is heard, they should ask for permission to modify the list of documents, and they should explain to the Judges how the document was obtained and why it wasn't included in the list beforehand. They should also explain why the document is so important that it has to be presented immediately in the course of the cross-examination. They must also explain why they cannot wait to present this document in the course of the rebuttal stage. Thirdly, my colleague said when the witness is in a position to assist the Chamber. But, Mr. President, since the very beginning of the Defence's case, we have noticed that on a number of occasions, the Prosecution has used the cross-examination not to challenge, not to contradict witnesses, but to find out names, find out things about certain events, and these are all matters that should have been dealt with before the commencement of the Defence's case. And finally, I'd like to draw your attention to this matter, Mr. President. When the Prosecution wants to produce a document, wants to show a witness a document, if it's a new document, it is obliged to show why it has a certain theory; they must explain their theory. They must say, Mr. Witness, Witness, I put it to you that such and such an event took place, and then, after having put their case to the witness, they can present their document. They can't go on a fishing expedition and show a document to a witness that might lead to a name and might lead to another name. As far as the credibility of a witness is concerned, Mr. President, this is something that we have already spoken about. This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is an exception. The Defence would never oppose the Prosecution if they wanted to use a document to discredit a witness and show that a witness gave false testimony. If someone gives false testimony, this is a very serious offence. And if the Prosecution wants to use any documents, new ones or old ones, they can show these documents to Defence counsel before the examination of the witness and say that they intend to use the document. We did this with a witness for the Prosecution, and we used a number of documents to demonstrate the particular situation that that witness was in. When we addressed the issue of the credibility of the witness, there's the credibility as a substantial issue, and there's credibility in the sense of the witness speaking the truth. In this particular case, the Prosecution may in fact present a new document. My colleague mentioned the Kupreskic case, and he mentioned a decision taken in the case dated 1999. As my colleague said, the purpose of this decision was to ensure that the accused weren't trapped, and it was also to ensure that the rights of the accused were respected. Nevertheless, Mr. President, this decision does not deal with new evidence. It does not state anything about the use of new documents to establish facts that should have been established in the course of the Prosecution's case. And that's the crux of the matter. The Prosecution shouldn't be granted leave to present new evidence in the course of the Defence's case. They have two occasions to do this, and that is during the presentation of its own case and during the rebuttal phase. As I have said, the Prosecution has all the resources it needs, and these resources have been used since 1993. If we compare their resources to the Defence counsel, well, you may think that the Defence counsel is very strong, but we don't have significant resources behind the scenes. Nothing that would be comparable to the resources that the Prosecution has. One final thing I would like to say, Mr. President, as far as the witnesses are concerned. The Prosecution says that our list of witnesses, we provided them a little too late, and they would like to know who is going to be called a week in advance. Naturally, we agree with the Prosecution, and we're doing our best, and we will continue to do our best in order to inform the Prosecution as soon as we have the relevant information about the identity of the future witnesses. Nevertheless, Mr. President, in the course of the Prosecution's case, we were faced with the identical situation. From one week to the next week, we didn't have the list of witnesses, and we didn't know the identity of the witnesses. Nevertheless, there's a huge difference. If the Defence doesn't know who the next witness is, this affects the rights of the accused. But in the case of the Prosecution, who have been involved in investigations for five years, if they only know about the witness' identity a few days in advance, well, this shouldn't affect them significantly. They have all the resources, they have all the investigators, they have all the documents, so the situation is different. Naturally, they might discover that the witness, or a witness has lied. Why should they prepare for a Defence witness? The Defence can prepare for a Prosecution witness, because the Prosecution witness will be appearing to testify and the evidence provided might establish the guilt of the accused. It's necessary to conduct a lot of investigations. But the Prosecution have already completed their investigations. They should be fully aware of the nature of their case. The problem in these proceedings is that the Prosecution appears to be unaware of the nature of their case, and we are wasting a lot of time as a result. And if I make submissions for 20 minutes, as well as my colleague, naturally we'll be wasting more time. But, Mr. President, it's necessary to spend this time in order to clarify the nature of the proceedings, because all the cases before the International Tribunal must show full respect for the rights of the accused. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Was there anything that the other Defence team would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There are a few points that we wish to add. Submissions by Mr. Dixon: Your Honours, if at the outset I could state that what my friend Mr. Mundis has said in two respects is absolutely correct. Firstly, that there is always a lot of new information that is potentially relevant to any case; and secondly, that it is not always possible for the Prosecution to foresee everything that the Defence is going to raise during its case. However, I think to be fair, Your Honours, there are important qualifications to be made to each of these points. Firstly, in respect of what the Prosecution can expect, it is correct that the Defence is required, under Rule 65 ter (F), to file a Defence statement at the commencement of the Prosecution case where the Defence sets out what its main lines of defence are going to be. So, for example, in the case of Mr. Kubura, I don't think that the Prosecution can complain that, from the outset, for example, in respect of the charges for Miletici and Malina, the Prosecution have known that the issue of the presence and the deployment of the 7th Brigade is the key issue in dispute; and that if they wish to prove their case in that respect, that is where they need to focus their efforts. In addition, throughout the whole Prosecution case, through the cross-examination that the Defence presents, the Prosecution is on notice as to what are the key challenges that are raised by the Defence. Secondly, Your Honours, in respect of the amount of information that does become available, in our submission, there must be some limit placed on the evidence that the Prosecution can use. Otherwise, trials would be elongated to unreasonable proportions. And also at the appeals stage, we would still be, as is the case in many appeals, looking at new evidence that does become available. And as Your Honours will know, the test for the admission of new evidence at the appeals stage is a very, very high one. Your Honours, Mr. Mundis is also correct that there is no rule which governs the disclosure of material to be used during cross-examination, and it is for each Trial Chamber to determine the matter according to its own procedures. We would urge Your Honours to be guided by Rule 89(B), which states that when there is no rule dealing with the issue in point, that Your Honours should devise a rule which best favours the fair determination of the matter before Your Honours. The touchstone is fairness. Of course, Your Honours, we are all concerned about determining the truth about what occurred in these proceedings, but that must be done in the context of a fair determination of the issues before Your Honours. We would, therefore, propose that a procedure be adopted which has four aspects to it. The first is that material can only be used in cross-examination when, as Mr. Mundis has said, it is disclosed at the earliest opportunity to the Defence. So disclosure is obviously the starting point. We can't be taken by surprise. That applies to both sides. Secondly, and this is the thrust of my submission, is that the disclosure must have taken place before the end of the Prosecution case, or at least before the start of the Defence case once the Defence begins calling its witnesses. The Prosecution has ample opportunity, and has had in this case, to extend the length of its case. If there are still documents coming in, well, more time can be asked for, if they are deemed to be relevant. For example, Your Honours, on the list of the document collections that is have been handed to you by Mr. Mundis, the third category, the ABiH security documents, I think many of the discussions we're having today are going to concern, in reality, these documents, which started coming in in February 2004 and finished in September 2004, which is just a little bit after the time when the Prosecution closed its case in July. And in our submission, there's no reason why, when those documents were coming in, an analysis couldn't have been made of them then, they could have been introduced during the Prosecution case, or more time could have been sought to extend the case so that those documents, which are potentially crucial documents, could be made available. For example, Witness ZP testified on the 14th of June and onwards, a member of the highest command within the Bosnian army, and would have been a witness through which many of these documents could have been considered and put before Your Honours. That's just one example, Your Honours, of how we say there must be a limit put on the extent of the documents the Prosecution can introduce. And we would say that that would be the end of the Prosecution case for such investigations and documents to be disclosed to the Defence. Your Honours, there are two exceptions, in our view. The one would be, and this is the third point of the procedure, if the Defence suddenly raises an entirely new defence not disclosed before and unforeseen, if we had to suddenly say, Well, Mr. Kubura was in Canada for 1993, Mr. Mundis would be justified in cross-examining our witnesses to introduce new documents to challenge that point, when there's no way he could have been on notice of that beforehand. But that would require the Prosecution to identify what is new, to make an application before Your Honours for those documents to be put in cross-examination, if -- this is, of course, only in a situation where those documents were not disclosed by the end of the Prosecution case. And the second issue Mr. Bourgon has referred to is the issue of credibility. We would, however, argue that credibility needs to be viewed in a very limited light. It's quite possible to cost any cross-examination of a witness as a challenge on credibility. And documents which are disclosed after the commencement of the Defence case, which support the Prosecution case, should not be put to a witness under the guise of credibility. Credibility only concerns a discrete allegation or statement made by a witness which can be challenged by a document which the Prosecution has only disclosed to the Defence at a much later stage, after the commencement of the Defence case. And it would be for the Prosecution to show how that document challenges the particular allegation made by the witness, how credibility is, therefore, an issue; and upon that application, for Your Honours to decide whether that document could be introduced. That would, of course, have to be done in the absence of the witness. So we would urge Your Honours to look at that in a narrow light. It shouldn't be used as a back door to fill gaps in the Prosecution case. And then lastly, Your Honours, the fourth aspect of the procedure is that any material the Prosecution obtains after the start of the Defence case that falls squarely under Rule 68 must be disclosed to the Defence. But once again, we would emphasise the back-door point. And this is not meant any disrespect to my friends. But material which is not truly Rule 68 should not be disclosed to the Defence in an effort, then, to say that the Defence have it so that it can then be used in cross-examination to introduce new evidence that the Prosecution wish to rely upon. If there's a critical point that has arisen in the Defence case, as has been stated, there's always the rebuttal stage to do that. Your Honours, that would be our proposed procedure to deal fairly with the matter before Your Honours, that all four of these steps be adopted. The key for us is that there must be some limit on what the Prosecution can continue to introduce as evidence, and the procedure adopted must be one which is fair to both the parties. The alternative would be that, conceivably, at the end of the Defence case, new material that hadn't been disclosed could still be introduced during the Defence case at a time when the entire case had already been presented to Your Honours. Your Honours, those are our submissions on this matter, and we would urge Your Honour to follow the spirit of Rule 89(D) in determining this matter. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will deliberate and we will render our decision as soon as possible. We are now going to bring in the witness, who must be wondering what's happening. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before the witness arrives, I'd just like to inform the Chamber that, following the motion filed by the Defence regarding the production of its list of documents, the Chamber orally informed us that we have up to the 3rd of December. We wish to remind you that in our request, we asked for 15 days after the disclosure of documents, and we can now confirm in the chamber that we received last night, or this morning, all the materials in the case against Prlic. There are 10.000 documents who are on the EDS system since yesterday. We shall do our best to review all those documents before the 3rd of December, and it is possible that we will be addressing the Chamber again if we fail to do so by the 3rd of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Please sit down. We kept you waiting, but we had to deal with a few problems before calling you in. The examination will continue. As we started at quarter past 2, we will go on until quarter to 4, for another 20 minutes, therefore, because then we will have to make a technical break. So we will have a break at a quarter to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answering my questions yesterday, you drew attention to a large number of obstacles that you had to grapple with, establishing the communications system for the 3rd Corps and the operations group. Will you tell me, please, should there have been breakdowns in the equipment, who would repair the military equipment within the communications system in the area in which you were operating?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these were minor repairs on the equipment, such as a break in the cable, then the people who were trained to operate the system would do the repairs. As for other repairs, they had to be done in the Maintenance Institute in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, Professor, you said that the devices that you had at your disposal came from different sources. Can you tell us which those sources were, and to what extent certain problems in repairing those devices were linked to their origins?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial Defence units at the time, and later army units, that is, brigades and units of the 3rd Corps, used similar sources for the provision of such devices. The main source were devices used by the former JNA to be found partly in the Maintenance Institute and partly in the warehouses which the units would capture on the ground. But percentage-wise, they had a very limited number of such devices. Then the second source were radio amateur equipment, and because they were used by radio hams, they were -- they could work under normal temperatures and could not tolerate major climatic changes. And a third source of devices were devices that had a special purpose, as I have already described. All those devices were not compatible; that is, at the beginning, they could not be used together. And as a result, we had to configure the radio network accordingly to deal with communication problems among the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Professor, how the system of communications functioned in the chain of command. How did the lower and higher commands communicate?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the concept that we tried to implement, we had several networks, and these were networks for control and command and networks for combat operations. The networks for control and command were used to issue -- for communications between subordinate and superior units, whereas the other networks were mainly used within units, and sometimes they could also be used for control and command, in certain special cases, for communicating with the superior command as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you said on a number of occasions that there would be breakdowns in the communications system. Tell me, were you a witness or are you aware of the way in which lower level commands endeavoured to bridge such breakdowns and to establish contact with a superior command, and what methods they used to do this?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases, when there are breakdowns in communication or in the lines between superior and subordinate units within a brigade or defence staffs, or between two brigades, it was customary to include in our communications plans such exceptional cases, that is, to use networks of higher commands. We had to convey the information to the higher command and then that command would use its network, which were radio links, to pass on that same information to a particular unit that it was intended for. So these are special links that were very complicated and difficult to use, because transmission of information was done through speech signals and this took a lot of time and required a lot of resources, and that was only the last resort, when we had no other way of conveying a telegramme or a message.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you, through a specific example, whether I fully understand your answer. If the 306th Brigade could not get in touch with its operations group, for instance, west of Krajina, how would it establish contact with that superior command? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command had its own network. It was a primary network in the system of control and command, and that network would have to be used. The telegraph would be sent through the communications centre of the 3rd Corps so that the communications unit of the 3rd Corps could forward that telegramme to the command of the operations group west, for instance. One could ask why this didn't function directly, because they were mostly radio communications. As cables -- cable wire links were broken at the very beginning, and also because of the configuration of the land, it is not always possible to find good quality radio channels, so that an intermediary has to be sought to deal with the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I think there is a misunderstanding somewhere. On page -- line 5, page 33, the witness is being asked if there's a breakdown in communication between a superior command and a subordinate unit, what happens, and the witness answers that in that event the superior command is informed which needs to contact the unit. However, in line 17, you're giving us an example, and you say, if the 306th Brigade could not get in touch with its operations group, what happens? But this is reversing the first question. Witness, let me ask you to be more specific, because it's important. The Defence is asking you, when there's a break in communications between the command and the subordinate unit, what happens? Can you answer that question? That was your question, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not following the transcript. My question was intended to give an example. So my question at first was, what happens if there's a breakdown between a subordinate unit and a superior command. And in answer to that question, the witness provided an answer. To make things clearer to me and everyone else, I gave a real example, an example that we heard from the witness, asking him to explain what happened, using the example of a particular brigade. Perhaps, Your Honour, it would be a good idea for the witness to clarify this, because if there was a problem in the translation of my question, this could cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of the problem, in my view, is the following: The 306th is a subordinate brigade to the operations group west, and if there is a breakdown in between the 306th and the operations group west, then the information is passed on to the command of the 3rd Corps, which is superior to the 306th Brigade and the operations group, and then, using primitive speech methods, the telegramme is forwarded to operations group west.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, could you tell me now something about the security of communications, and to what extent your system, in the 3rd Corps, or rather, in the operations group where you worked in the second half of 1993, to what extent that system was protected from disturbances by enemy forces, and jamming.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that we used conventional devices which are highly susceptible to interception, and the former JNA would develop special devices which used to be a part of the set to provide cryptographic protection. In the area covered by the units and command of the 3rd Corps, we did not, in that period of time, have a single system or any additional encrypting device to provide protection from interception of our communications. So there was no way we could deal with this, so that the technology of the devices that we used was highly susceptible to interference and interception.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in view of the fact that in 1993 there were major combat operations between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, do you know, and if you do, how, which devices and resources the HVO had at their disposal to intercept the communications system of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. In May and June '92, I was the initiator and, to a certain extent, the designer of a system. We used a military vehicle, a TAM 150, using measuring devices. In the Travnik Maintenance Institute, we developed quite a sophisticated system for reconnaissance. And it was based, the equipment itself was suitable for computerisation. And this system was located, by agreement, to the area controlled by the HVO. So after the first conflicts and disagreements started, this system was left to the HVO, and our operators did not have access to that centre. I wish to underline that the location was technically not the most suitable, but it was accepted, simply to meet the requests of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When a highly sophisticated device, as you describe it, was given to the HVO, what was the plan for the use of that device, since we're talking about 1992, when you were operating as allies?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system was designed to be mobile, on a vehicle, and by selecting the proper locations and using well-trained operators, the system could monitor all radio networks; our own networks, as well as the networks of the Serb units in the territory or the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and the area of responsibility of the HVO. We're talking about the area around Vlasic, Zenica, the Lasva Valley, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, in answer to my questions, you spoke about a system of communications that was to satisfy the operative tactical needs, as well as those required at the combat level. Could you please clarify, what is the tactical level and what is the combat level?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every army, every concept that includes preparation of combat operations, has to provide secure communications, so that the combat level covers a smaller area, an area in which battles are fought, where there are combat activities between units, up to the level of company or battalion. And for this purpose, special frequency ranges are used and a special device. Those devices, depending on the location and the configuration of the land, could even be used for the tactical level. However, the tactical level is provided with different devices and different frequency ranges, and are used mainly to monitor combat operations, to report about those operations, and to pass on information during the preparation stage for combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you were an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, and you worked on communications. As a university professor, you are familiar with the NATO communications system as well. Tell us what quantity of resources you used for the communications system of the 3rd Corps. Were they up to the standards of the Yugoslav army or NATO standards? If not, tell us how well-equipped the 3rd Corps was in the course of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, as a member, or as an employee of the Defence Ministry, I was a coordinator and collaborated with experts of the US army regarding communications for control and command, so that I was aware of the NATO norms and standards. And I knew the JNA standards. And many were surprised how we managed, with limited resources that we had, to ensure the necessary level of communications. And taking into account both concepts, I think a maximum of 15 per cent existed in relation to the normal requirements for communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We better stop. We are going to stop, because it's more than a quarter to 4.00, and we will resume at about 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence so that they can continue with their examination now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just before the break, you were saying that, up until the end of 1993, the 3rd Corps had 15 per cent of communications equipment at the most, equipment that would fit the norms and the standards of the former JNA. The system that you developed in 1993, in the 3rd Corps, to what extent did it meet the norms for providing communications, if you compared the situation with the JNA or with NATO?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, I've already answered that question. As far as protecting those communications is concerned, as far as cryptographic methods is concerned, as far as intercepting and jamming the communications system, the percentage was a lot lower. You could say that the communications system was never adequately protected or secured from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in order to clarify what you have just said, to a certain extent, I would like to ask you what the usual norms would have been, if we're talking about the JNA or some NATO army, what would have been the lowest level if someone might have been using a radio set? Would this concern a platoon, a company, an individual?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have a look at the structure or the organisation of the former JNA, well, it would be a detachment. All detachment commanders should have had a certain communications device. This depended on the tasks that they had to carry out. Naturally, certain soldiers should also have the possibility of establishing communications, because they carry out additional tasks outside the scope of platoons, for example. So this would be the minimum that would have to be provided to develop communications systems for commanding and controlling units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if we assume that there are at least 100 platoons in one brigade, one brigade consists of at least 100 platoons, what would you say, were there 100 radio devices at any point in time in any of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one would have to rephrase your question, because one device doesn't mean anything on its own. We can talk about the activities that involve a number of devices. We call this system radio directions. The only way to make up for the lack of equipment, for the lack of devices, and it wasn't possible to obtain a sufficient number of devices, the only way to make up for the lack of equipment was as follows: First of all, you needed a high level of training for the operators, for the men, for the commanders, who provided communications. And secondly, there was redistribution. We spent a lot of time and a lot of resources on using equipment that was used in one centre, in another centre, so we would relocate equipment from one centre to another centre. So these criteria were never fulfilled. Far from it. And I've told you how it was possible to make up for the lack of equipment. In the case of areas where there was no combat, we would take equipment from those areas. But units would sometimes be left without the basic means of communications. This was because we thought it was necessary to use the equipment they had in areas where it was more important to have that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just said that you paid a lot of attention to training men. Could you tell us who trained these communications officers, these men who operated the equipment?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, training was organised in the following manner: For radio amateurs -- for radio amateur equipment and radio amateur technology, we had men who were familiar with this technology, who were involved in the training. These devices, this equipment, was in army units, and there were men who could assist with the training. And then the commanders would train subordinate units. So there was a lot of attention that was paid to training and instructing units and individuals who were in the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever helped by foreigners or Mujahedin in providing training for communications devices?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I knew enough and I could use my knowledge to instruct others. Given my experience and the job I had, the people could be trained who had to use devices for tactical reasons. It was never necessary to have that kind of assistance. We never used assistance provided by the Mujahedin or any individuals who were outside the 3rd Corps system.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these Mujahedin ever used the army communications system for their own purposes, to carry out activities of their own, or for any other needs?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never had any contact with them. I don't know how they dealt with those problems. But I can assume that they probably tried to resolve those difficulties. But as to the equipment they had, I don't know, they didn't have any army equipment. As to whether they bought equipment or obtained equipment in some way, I don't know. But they couldn't have used such equipment if they didn't have adequate and appropriate instructors.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on the basis of documents we have seen, we realise that documents were often forwarded by packet communications. Please, could you tell us whether packet communications were used within the communications system of the 3rd Corps, and what did this mean, exactly? How did this function?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first tell you what packet communications involves. Packet communications is a system that uses an intermediary to transfer information. In order to use such a system, you need to have a computer on both sides with appropriate modems; you need a station that emits; then you need an intermediary that functions as a sort of transit point for the information. This was a system developed for radio amateurs. So, radio amateurs developed this technology. We realised what the potential for such technology was in the conditions that prevailed at the time. And we only introduced this technology in cases where it was appropriate to use this technology. It meant that you needed premises where the temperature was 20 degrees and where the humidity was 50 per cent. That enabled you to use the system. So this technology was used to provide communications in the field. Naturally, this technology is used as part of the modern equipment of all armies now. But at the time, it was a technology that was only used by radio amateurs. We introduced, to a certain extent, at the beginning of 1993, in March, April, and May, we introduced this equipment and trained our operators to use this technology. We trained people at the level of the 3rd Corps in order to be able to establish communications between the brigades and the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that that communications system required an intermediary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you need a point, a reference point in space that has a connection with both -- that can see both users in order to be able to provide an efficient way of communicating information via that link.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that up until May you were busy introducing that system. To what level within the army was this system of packet communications introduced, up until the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was introduced between commands and brigades to the extent it was used in operations groups, and also for communications between brigades and the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as relaying information is concerned, what could you tell us about the technology that was required to verbally relay information?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an interesting question. Usually, telegrammes provide the contents of information, and that's how they should be treated. Special systems should be used to relay such information, for example, packet communications. But given the lack of such equipment in the units and in the commands, we would encode a telegramme or document and this coded message would then be transmitted verbally over radio channels. And we used the frequencies that were available to relay this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did one communications centre work for a certain level of command? For example, the communications centre of the 3rd Corps, for a brigade, for how long was it in operation?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these communications centres worked around the clock. All posts had to be occupied around the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One communications centre, for example, at the level of brigade, within a brigade, what sort of possibilities did it have? Was it possible for such a communications centre to establish a number of connections at the level of the 3rd Corps, for example? You've just mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could provide you with an example. Imagine two towns, and you have a crossroads and vehicles arrive from five or six directions. And you have another town with a similar junction, and you have a similar volume of traffic at that junction in the second town. So if the extent of traffic between those two centres involves 10-lane motorways, then it's not a problem, circulation between those two centres for the vehicles is not a problem. And that is the case for communications, too. It all depended on the number of channels you had available in order to provide such a communications system. Given the lack of devices, given the limited number of devices that we had, and given the limited number of centres, on the whole, only one channel was used. So you had a link with the superior command, and you used the same equipment you used for links with subordinate commands. So you first had to finish relaying communication to the superior command, and then you would use the equipment to relay information to subordinate units. This is a very complicated and difficult job because you need operators who are very experienced and very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, in such situations, how sure can one be that a message sent from one command level will be received by the person to whom the message is sent, especially since we know about all the problems that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, if we're talking about the relay of information via speech, and I've already described how this worked, then this system is not very reliable, and its reliability diminishes if you use a circular method of work. At the station that is the central source of information, that distributes information to a number of users who are using the same Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. channel, well, in such cases it's difficult for them to confirm whether a message has been received. So the technology for relaying information in a reliable manner, well, it's difficult to provide such technology, to provide information in a reliable manner in the conditions that prevailed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if we look at the way in which this communications system was developed, and if we look at the possibilities of communicating between superior and subordinate commands, could you tell me, to what extent did this system function in this way in 1993, up to which level did it function in this way? How well-established were the links up to the level of battalions -- at the level of battalions, companies, and platoons?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation changed, depending on the deployment of the commands or units that were carrying out combat operations, defence or attack operations. If you examine the overall situation, I think that a brigade always had, perhaps, up to about one-third of the equipment necessary. They had such equipment by using the resources and applying the principles that I mentioned, the principles that involved redistributing equipment and redistributing devices. Sometimes individual units were islands, so to speak, isolated islands, because they or the superior command wasn't able to provide communications. In Vlasic, this is something that frequently happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although these questions concerning equipment and communications are certainly extremely complicated -- and I am not in a position to ask you all the questions I would like to ask you about these matters, and I'd like to thank you for your answers -- I'd like to move onto something else. In 1993, did you assume any other duties, or rather, were you assigned any other tasks, apart from the task in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, towards the end of April or at the beginning of May, I was transferred to the joint command for Central Bosnia. This command was transferred to the joint command for Central Bosnia. This command was composed of army members and of HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the help of the usher, I would now like to show the Professor a number of documents. My next questions will have to do -- my following questions will have to do with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, will you please look at document number 5 and tell me whether that document is actually information about that particular function of the new joint command, of which you are a member.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just information to corps in the operation zone for Central Bosnia, just an announcement to tell them that the command has started operating and its composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the command based?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the post office of Travnik, in the basement of that building in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the main task of that command?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main task of the command was to plan operations against the common enemy in the areas of responsibility of both commands, planning operations by the joint forces of the HVO and the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, the document I showed you is Defence Exhibit DH159. Will you now look at 0995, Defence Exhibit 0995. Professor, does this document speak of the assignment that you personally assumed in the command.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was responsible for ensuring the system of communications for this temporary command structure, and as the command of the 3rd Corps and of the HVO in Vitez could communicate through the public system of communications, we insisted that that be the first step in establishing communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now will you please look at documents number 3 and number 4. They are DH Exhibits 996 and 081 -- 996 and 981.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my activities in the joint command, or rather, my cooperation, who was to be my partner in the HVO, we were supposed to work together in establishing these communications, and I feel that the person attached to our command did not have the necessary knowledge or skills for these assignments. So there were quite a number of problems due to this, and as a result, I agreed that the public enterprise PPT Travnik should introduce mobile telephony in this area. This was a concession so as to get a response from an institution that was the only one capable. But this could not be done because it was not possible to develop mobile telephony during the war. It was only after the war that it was introduced in Bosnia-Herzegovina this was established. So the concept was doomed to fail. It was never achieved. But this was simply a concession, telling those who could provide a qualified answer what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me to look at this other document.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is simply a request, as we wanted to deal with packet -- package networks through the system we have just described. We asked for personnel from army units and the HVO to operate these communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a representative of the BH army in this joint command, how did you undertake preparations for joint operations, and what was the approach taken by our colleagues from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who have an understanding of these things and who are monitoring developments in the world of communications, especially military communications, know that, using mobile telephony from public institutions doesn't have much use. And the aims set could never be realised, because no serious problem was addressed using methods applied in all armies. So this communications problem, too, was not addressed as seriously as it should have been. The work of the command was mainly based on complaints, mostly by one side, and then teams were formed to go into the field to analyse the situation there. I joined the command with a clear task to plan combat operations against a joint enemy rather than to deal with problems that occur in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After your work in the joint command, or rather, let me ask you: Did that command function successfully, or was it brought to the end precisely because of the obstruction you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we examine the aim of the joint command, I think that its results were equal to zero. Nothing was done that the joint command was supposed to do. As for the other aspect, I was not a member of those commissions that went into the field so -- as I had other things to do. But I think as far as its prime goal was concerned, the joint command did not achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Professor, after your work in the joint command, which, as you said, never even started to work properly, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this assignment, I took over the duty ahead of communications of the operations group Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that position, did you manage at some point in time to decipher any HVO messages? If you did, tell us which, and were they important for the command and for the protection of defence lines?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the events in Travnik, that is, the conflict and the attack operations of the HVO in the broader area of Travnik, we tried and managed to monitor their radio communications using standard military equipment and some additions and support from computers. We had well-trained people, people who were skilled in these disciplines, that is, in computerisation, so that certain encryption systems used by the HVO were broken into and we managed to decode the contents of those messages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a specific example of which you informed your commander, that is, the links that existed between two enemies at that point in time, two enemies of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a couple of telegrammes, the contents of which revealed contacts between the Serbian side and the HVO at the level of brigade commands; also, about certain movement of units and activities in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. It is very interesting that both parties should use the same system of encryption. Even though it was primitive, what it meant was that they could develop a joint encryption system that they used in their mutual communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, where was your communications centre of the operations group Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the events that took place in the area of Travnik, and because the operations group did not have its own communications resources, we used the equipment of the 17th Vitez Brigade, and parallel with the communications centre in the basement of the Travnik barracks, we developed a centre for monitoring and analysing traffic between both sides, in that same building; that is, we monitored traffic as far as we were able, with the technology we had. All the personnel was housed in the basements of barracks for the simple reason that it was not possible to go outside because of sniping and mortar shelling from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, how much time did you spend in the communications centre in the Travnik barracks?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the conflict and during and after, since there was an HVO unit on a hill above Travnik which was able to target the barracks, I spent my entire time in the basement, because it wasn't possible to go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see on those premises other parts of the basement that were used as prisons?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the corridors were close to one another, I could hear the guards. And as I knew the premises from before, as that is where I did my military service, I knew that there were some kind of prison premises there, and we knew that they existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, as you spent time in that basement, did you ever hear or see anyone mistreating the persons who were being held there, in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't talk about the detention area itself specifically, but I never heard, nor did I have any inkling that anything like that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to my colleague. Because of the translation, there's an error. Maybe there's imprecision in the interpretation, because the professor says that he didn't know what was happening. It says here "detention area itself specifically." I'm not sure that that reflects what the professor said. Maybe I should repeat my question so as to get a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the cells?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I would pass along the corridors. On one side were the cells, and on the other side were the premises that we used. I would come there at any time of day and night, when information could be exchanged. So all I can say is I did not see or hear anything strange happening. And if I didn't know, I wouldn't be able to tell that those areas were being used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During your testimony, I think page 34, and the Presiding Judge raised the issue, when there's a breakdown of communications between command and subordinate units, let me ask you, when we're talking about the brigade and the battalion, when there's a breakdown in communications between the brigade command and the battalions of that brigade -- you probably know that there were three battalions of the Muslim Brigade, and that the command was in Zenica. I think the same applied to the 314th Brigade. Bearing everything in mind that you said regarding problems with communications that occurred, what was the situation like in Travnik in May and June of 1993? Could you describe this situation, that is, the relationship between the brigade and the battalions.
