utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the configuration of the land, Travnik is very unsuitable for establishing any kind of communications on frequencies, and you have to use the high frequency range, which is a range which is extremely unsuitable, where disturbances are such during the day and night that you have to plan communications very carefully. And unlike others, we didn't have special services for planning such channels. NATO has a special service for the frequency management of this kind, so they, too, had to use our resources, that is, to relay telegrammes to special communication channels to the brigade command. They had to use the same technology, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript. In Travnik there was only one battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, whereas the command was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When describing this situation, you used the term "isolated island," a situation when the command cannot establish communication with its subordinate battalion. Would you say that the 1st Battalion, in relation to the brigade command in Zenica, was in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in such a situation very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also confirm that between the brigade and the battalion, there was no packet communications?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, the brigade and the battalion did not have a packet link. That's for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Darryl Mundis, and together with my colleagues, we represent the Prosecution here today. I'm going to ask you a few questions. I just wanted to make sure at the beginning, sir, that you understand that my purpose is not in any way to confuse you, and if there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, simply tell me that and I will rephrase the question so that you do understand that. Is that clear? You were just telling us, in response to some questions from my learned colleague, that communications between the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and its 1st Battalion, you characterised as an isolated island, or you said it was in such a situation very frequently. What time period were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can refer to the entire period, up until the point in time when equipment was available to solve the problems, that is to say, up until the time when the operations group managed to establish a fully efficient system of command and control. So that was the situation that prevailed in the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it, then, that in the second half of 1993, this problem was largely solved?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was solved. It was in the process of being solved, because as far as communications is concerned, as far as the technology we had available is concerned, well, we could never say that the problems had been solved. According to the terminology we use, we can talk about the reliability of the communications system. At that period of time, the situation was better. When the operations group established a system of command and command and control, the situation was better. I think that would be in August, or at the beginning of September, and afterwards. Why was the situation improved? Well, because we redistricted certain equipment in order to improve the system, in order to improve the functioning within those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me talk, then, sir, about the first part of 1993, that is, up until, as you put it, the end of August or beginning of September, so let's talk about the period from January until the end of August 1993. And again, because we were talking about the 7th Battalion -- the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and its 1st Battalion, let's focus on that relationship, if you will. During that period, from January through the end of August 1993, how reliable, in your professional estimate, was communication between that battalion and the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I put it in the following way: If you made 10 attempts to establish communications, or there was a request to transfer telegrammes, perhaps you would be successful in one or two cases. So if you had 24 hours to use your communications systems, and you had 10 telegrammes, during that period of time, you could perhaps forward two telegrammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit -- now I'm talking in general terms, in 1993, throughout that year, within the 3rd Corps as a whole, based on your experience there and your professional expertise, the communications systems, and I use the word plural, "systems," meaning all the range of communications means available, would you call that system or those systems, in 1993, functional or dysfunctional?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say, if I examined the system and the men involved, and I believe that a lot of attention was paid to training men and a lot of attention was paid to manoeuvring equipment, or rather, we tried to move equipment from one area to another area, from one unit to another unit, so that functioned -- from that point of view, it was functioning. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But if we held onto our resources, our equipment, without relocating the equipment, in that case, I wouldn't say that the system functioned. It was possible for the system to function because the equipment was relocated very frequently, and a lot of attention was paid to training the men who are involved in providing the communications system. Let me explain to you what I mean by "manoeuvre." For example, a combat operation at place X is planned, then I would get hold of all the equipment at that location, for example, mobile devices, other devices that aren't used at the time, and then I would provide these units with this equipment, together with the relevant orders. They would carry out their task and use that equipment. And when it was decided that the equipment was no longer needed, the equipment had to be returned and sent back to the locations where they were taken from. This was a very complicated procedure, but it was the only manner in which we could operate during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about the time period where you were with -- you told us yesterday there came a time when you were part of the communications battalion of the 3rd Corps. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the time period, or the approximate time period, that you were part of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the corps was formed sometime in November, and I assumed my new duties in the joint command in Central Bosnia somewhere around the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it, then, sir, that for approximately six months, from November 1992 through May 1993, you were with the 3rd Corps communications battalion; is that approximately correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During that period, approximately how many men were in the communications battalion of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, in terms of the establishment, it was the battalion that -- as far as the strength of the battalion is concerned, well, I wasn't a member of the personnel staff, so I don't know the exact numbers, but it wasn't up to full strength. One couldn't speak about a real communications battalion. I think it was, in terms of its strength, more like a company, but it was described as a battalion because that's what it was supposed to be, according to its establishment. But perhaps there were as many men as one would have in a company, up to about a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where were these men, these men of the communications battalion, where were these men deployed during the six-month period you were part of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were deployed at various locations and in the communications centre of the 3rd Corps. My task wasn't that of an operations officer, or rather, I didn't have the task of an operator. I had to design the network, assist with training, introduce new devices, new equipment, et cetera, et cetera. I had a team that worked with me in the Travnik Maintenance Institute and they were members of that battalion. They carried out tasks in the wide area of the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and they had a unit in the corps command, and parts of the unit would accompany subordinate units and go there with the relevant equipment. In the case of units that didn't have their own equipment, resources were provided and the technical means were provided to have communications with those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps my question wasn't clear, but I was more interested about the geographic areas within the 3rd Corps zone where members of the communications battalion were stationed or deployed. Let's take yourself as a starting point. You remained in Travnik during the six-month period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Zenica and in Travnik and in the surrounding hills and mountains. I was in the command of the 306th, the command of the 312th, the command of the 314th, et cetera. I was present in units where it was necessary to help, where it was necessary to provide equipment and train the men to carry out their tasks. I wasn't the battalion commander. So as to where the units were deployed, et cetera -- well, as a rule, I know the areas that they were in, but I wouldn't really go into that, I wouldn't really go into where they were deployed. But I know the principles that were followed and I know how that unit was used and I know how the resources of that unit were used. Perhaps I should clarify something with regard to the training of units, or rather, with regard to the training of men that had to provide the communications system for command and control. They had to be trained to use devices, they had to be trained to use cryptographic machines, they had to be trained in procedures that had to be followed when sending and receiving telegrammes, et cetera. So their tasks were quite varied. And they also had to maintain the equipment, because the communications battalion also had units that first came into contact with faulty equipment, and they had to deal with this problem at their own level, and to the extent that it was possible for them to deal with these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the period of time when you were with the 3rd Corps communications battalion, who was the commander of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander was, he is a brigadier now, his name was Senad Salimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period when you were with the communications battalion of the 3rd Corps, did you, on any occasion, have the opportunity to discuss communications issues with the 3rd Corps commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have any significant form of contact with the general, but I was a member of the delegation from the Maintenance Institute that went to see the general when we had to resolve certain difficulties that concerned the security and protection of the institute itself. And the problems also concerned the functioning of the Maintenance Institute in Travnik and the maintenance of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question, though, sir, was did -- on these occasions, you said you did not have any significant form of contact. Did the 3rd Corps commander ever raise with you problems concerning the communications systems in place within the 3rd Corps during the time period you were part of the 3rd Corps communications battalion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, my task didn't involve the command and control of that battalion, and I believe that the general was a trained officer and he knew what the role of the communications system was. As far as dealing with the problems of command and control are concerned, I assume that he had contact with the commander and issued tasks to the commander. I didn't receive any tasks from the commander himself. But on the other hand, if we examine the way in which we worked, and if we examine the possibilities we had, well, we had carte blanche to do whatever we could do in those conditions to ensure that the system of command and control functioned properly. So a commander can't show more confidence in his subordinates, or this is the best way for a commander to show that he has confidence in his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you said "we had carte blanche to do whatever we could do in those conditions to ensure that the system of command and control functioned properly." And I ask you, in this context, did you do everything possible to ensure that this system worked?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what I myself think about this. When all this came to an end, I've often thought about this matter and about that time period. I wouldn't want such a thing to ever happen again. I wouldn't want to go back to that time, because it was a very difficult situation. Well, if you are someone who has a certain proficiency, certain knowledge, and you don't have the means of doing what you know how to do, this is a difficult situation. I admire people who did what they did in those conditions, in the rear, the combat line, et cetera. And so I think in that respect, we did our utmost, we did our best, and I myself did all I could in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return to a theme that we spoke about a few moments ago. The battalion -- the 3rd Corps communications battalion commander, Mr. Salimovic, do you recall ever discussing with him any complaints that he received from the commander of the 3rd Corps about specific communication problems?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had frequent and direct contact with the commander, who was a colleague of mine, because after my duties as chief of communications, I became the chief of communications in a corps. All the time we understood each other and cooperated well. Mr. Salimovic was responsible for tactical matters, for the use of units. I was responsible for preparing the men and the technology. He would receive tasks, but I was only interested in the tasks to the extent that they concerned me and my team, or rather, the team who carried out the tasks assigned to us, along with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, if you recall, where you were or what unit you were assigned to on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the documents, on paper at least, I think I was still listed as a member of this joint command. You know, I don't remember receiving an order relieving me of those duties. I only received an order appointing me to my new duties in the operations group. So I had a certain authority in the joint command -- because of what I had done in the joint command, I also had certain authority in the units that were communication units. So I was still listed officially as a member of that joint command. I never received a document in which I was relieved of those duties during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can recall, where were you physically present on 8 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of all the circumstances, I can't really give you a precise answer regarding that date. But in that period of time, I was in Travnik. That was when these activities was going on and the conflict with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it, sir, from the last sentence of your answer that you were, therefore, aware that there was a relatively high degree of military operations going on in the Bila valley on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your conclusion is correct, because, as a member of the joint command and listening to complaints and following those developments, because we had meetings with the commands and commanders of units and operations groups, I was aware of what was going on. But as the joint command was housed in that building in Travnik, I felt personally the consequences of those conflicts. I couldn't leave the building. We used all kinds of methods to move from the barracks when we had to; in the dark, at night, and so on. So as someone who lived and worked with people in the joint command, as someone who lived in Travnik, I knew what was going on. On the other hand, from contacts and the presentation of those events that I heard about at meetings from Commander Alagic, Cuskic, and the representatives of the HVO, I knew what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, and I would like your comments on what I'm about to suggest, that the operations undertaken by units of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH on 8 June 1993 in the Bila valley reflected a relatively high degree of tactical command and control, and a relatively high degree of communications were necessary for those military operations to be successful.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said yourself that the operations were in the Bila valley, and I spoke about the techniques and the principles and the efforts we made to have well-trained personnel, that we regrouped equipment. But I think that I couldn't describe the functioning of that segment as being particularly effective, nor did the system of communications have a very significant contribution. We also applied the same techniques and methods, and our contribution was always up to a maximum level, as far as the use of the technology allowed. But I wouldn't really describe our contribution in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn back now, sir, to the earlier period, and I'm referring to the summer of 1992. You told us yesterday, at that point in time, that among the jobs or the tasks that you had when you were with the Territorial Defence was supplying communications systems to the Territorial Defence and HVO units. Did I understand ...

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't. That was my assignment as director of the Maintenance Institute in Travnik. And when officers of the former JNA left the institute, and after the Presidency gave the decision that I should be provisional manager, I carried out those tasks as instructed by the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what time period was this that you're now referring to?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the period from May until, shall we say, July, end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question, sir, is: How did you -- how was the physical process of supplying the Territorial Defence units and the HVO units undertaken? Did people from those units come to the institute and retrieve the equipment, or did you deliver it to various locations? How did that actually work?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How it worked was that, as the provisional manager of the institute, I would receive instructions from the Presidency. I wouldn't call it an order, but instructions for certain means, indicating the name and the quantity should be given to the units, and then representatives of those units would come. And as I said yesterday, I was not informed at all about how the HVO units were equipped. But we simply carried out the instructions given by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it, then, from your answer, sir, that the representatives of the units came to the institute and collected the equipment and took it back to the units.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "mostly so," do you recall any specific incidents or time periods where you, or persons from the institute, went to the unit with radio equipment and delivered it or delivered it and installed it? Do you recall any incidents or instances where that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would avoid giving instructions to subordinates, that is, personnel from the institute, to go to the units, and I don't remember of any such cases. But I do remember other cases when units, especially HVO units, would, from positions of power, insist and pressure me to speed up the procedure and to resolve the problem of distribution of equipment. And I have to tell you that in that period of time, when all this was taking place, this transitional period for the institute, the HVO units wanted to gain full control of the institute. And I remember a positive example, Major Mihajlo Petrovic, who unfortunately was killed as a member of the BH army in 1993, thanks to whose courage and behaviour, the problem was resolved and HVO units were prevented from entering the premises where the equipment was held, and to keep both outside the working premises and the warehouses of the institute. In that transitional period, we would use a squad of the HVO and the army to provide physical protection of the buildings of the institute, which are quite large, because of the possibility of reserve units, who were located next door to the former barracks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, just so that we're clear, other than units of the Territorial Defence, units of the HVO, and later, units of the 3rd Corps, would it be correct that the institute did not provide any type of communications equipment to any other person, entity, agency, governmental office, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in answering your question, I would like to say precisely that we did not give equipment to anyone else while I was receiving instructions from the War Presidency. Of course, there were certain contacts with state institutions, and the institute later received instructions from the Defence Ministry, and on the basis of those instructions, it did distribute equipment. As for those instructions, as I still dealt with the institute, I am not aware that they distributed that equipment in that way, nor could they do that. The institute continued to function and provided services for other systems, for the electricity boards, et cetera, because we had a large generator, for instance, so it was working on a sort of commercial basis in the sense of exchange of goods. But apart from that, I can't give you a more precise answer. And if there were any requests of that kind, they must have been outside the institutions. From the moment the operations group was formed, and when I took up my new duties, and while I was in the joint command, I didn't do anything outside the system, nor did I send or coordinate any other units or individuals or institutions in terms of supplying them with equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So let me turn to the last subject I want to ask you about. I have just a couple of questions about this. You were asked earlier today about your knowledge concerning persons who were being kept in the basement of the barracks where you were assigned or stationed. Can you please describe for us where those persons were kept, perhaps starting with going down the stairs into the basement of that building, and where you were going. You told us that you passed by that corridor on your way somewhere else. Can you just tell us, to the best of your recollection, as you go down the stairs and into the basement, where those persons were being kept and where you were going.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would turn right, and these areas were to the left. So as soon as I turned right, there would be a soldier who acted as a sort of guard, and the corridor was open. There wasn't a door. There was a corridor that was used generally. And I think that answers your question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. As for the details, who was there and what they were doing, my role and function was such that I had no interest in that, so I cannot give you any details. But it may be interesting to note, there was an intervention by one of my staff. He used to be my driver in the institute, and his wife was the treasurer. And during the conflict, a young man, Adzaip, was held in detention, and I guarantee that he was someone who hadn't done any serious offence, so I intervened personally with persons who were in charge. Now, whether it was Beba Salko, I'm not quite sure, or General Alagic in person. They believed me. And that is the only case I can comment on when talking about those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it, sir, then, from the answer that you just gave us, that based upon your representations to Salko Beba or General Alagic, this individual was released?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of follow-on questions from my previous question about the corridor. When you get to the bottom of the stairs in the barracks building, you would turn right to go to the communications centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we say right? Probably right, because those corridors in the basement, I haven't been there for a long time. Must be 10 or 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the persons who were being kept there were to the left, at the bottom of the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pass by. My route didn't take me next to those areas, those premises. So the corridor was an area that led both to the basement area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That was actually my point, sir. When you were going down to the basement, to the communications room, you didn't actually walk in front of the rooms where these persons were being kept.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just saying that the corridors were such, and I would certainly have noticed or been able to identify had there been anything unusual. I said that I did not enter those cells. It didn't interest me. I was someone who had to spend a lot of time there because of my duties, so had anything happened there, be it during the day or the night, I would have heard it, because you can hear it. It's not so far away that one wouldn't notice any unusual sounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 5.35. We'll have a technical break. We will resume around 6.00. I will give the floor to the Defence for their re-examination, and after that, the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to Defence for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you said how you distributed equipment in the Maintenance Institute, where you were the director in July 1992. Could you please tell me whether, in that year, all the equipment that the institute had was distributed to the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the purpose, the function, of the institute, which was to maintain equipment, at the time we shared out all the equipment that was in good working order, all the equipment that could be used. Naturally, a certain amount of equipment remained in the warehouses. This was faulty equipment which had to be repaired so that the device could work properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said, Professor, that the main purpose of the institute was to repair and maintain those systems. Would I be correct if I said that the Maintenance Institute didn't produce communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institute never produced communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not necessary to go into further detail. Thank you. You've answered my question. My learned colleague also asked you whether the communication system that was established in the 3rd Corps could be considered to be functional. You mentioned the staff, the importance of the staff and the importance of having mobile equipment in order to ensure that the system was functional, to a certain extent. My question, Professor, is: Since you spoke about training men to deal with certain elements within the communications system, could you tell me whether the -- the way in which the system functioned also depended on the level of training provided to the men?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the equipment at hand, given what was available to us, it was essential to train men. We had organised activities to train these men. This is what we focused on in order to raise the level of combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us, given the level of training that the men had, given their ability to use the system at the end of 1993, to what extent was the communications system better at the end of 1993 in relation to the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say that it was better because some equipment had been captured. In spite of these developments, the number of resources that could be used, or the amount of resources used didn't significantly change, so the efficiency was the same as in 1993. What guaranteed the efficient functioning of the system was the men, or rather, the mobility of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Towards -- or rather, the men, towards the end of 1993, did they have more knowledge, were their possibilities greater, were they able to put the equipment they had to better use, towards the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that towards the end of 1993, they had attained the level of skill that was necessary for them to efficiently use the communications equipment that they had available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has drawn my attention to something in line 23, page 70, a translation. It doesn't have to do with mobile equipment here, it has to do with equipment that one could distribute via manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you could relocate equipment when needed. Thank you. I think it's clear in the transcript now. In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you mentioned the problems the commanders had as far as the communications system was concerned. Could you just tell me now, the communications battalion that you were a part of, was this attached to the unit or was it a unit that was attached to the commander?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the rules that we followed, this unit should have been under the command of the commander. It had the nature of a unit attached to it that, in practice, as far as planning was concerned for the use of the unit, the chief of staff could also have command over that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned numerous problems that you were confronted with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now show the witness Exhibit P192.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, it's a report from the 3rd Corps commander. Have a look at the middle of the document. It's entitled "The Problems of Command and Control." The number is 01851600. That's the number for the B/C/S version. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the last paragraph that commences with the words "The second problem," or "The other problem," and go to the next page to the section where it says "Certain limits," and then tell me whether this reflects the state of the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The second problem has to do with the communications system for command and control. This problem is also present at the level of companies and platoons. So companies may carry out attacks, but the companies may not have a radio or a link with the platoon commander. They will only have a career link. One must admit that the career link isn't efficient if the enemy has better communications systems. One must admit that a career link is not sufficiently efficient if the enemy, the aggressor, has better communications equipment, and if his units can be manoeuvred more easily." I'll now go to the other page. "This problem is particularly present when carrying out attacks. If a platoon is engaged in an attack on a given axis, which is fairly broad, and if the platoon commander has no links with the left and right flank --" well, I won't even mention the problem of cooperation, regardless of the way it any it's established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This description of the problems at that level of command, were these the kind of problems that you were aware of as someone who was involved in that field? Was this the problem throughout the area covered by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This reflects the actual situation in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, my colleague also asked you about certain communications in the course of combat in June 1993. Tell me, at the time, were you faced with the problem of a total lack of communications with certain units in the area of combat, and if so, could you tell us which units are concerned, and if this did occur, how could you obtain essential information on the events unfolding?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually there were breaks in communication with the 306th Brigade, because the brigade itself was located in terrain, the configuration of which was not suitable for radio links. And the post office infrastructure wasn't very good, and when there was such an infrastructure, it would fall into disrepair. So usually we would deal with these breaks in communication by establishing communication with the superior command in the communications centre of the superior command. But it's also important to note that those units had communication problems in the zone that they covered, or rather, in the zone where they engaged in combat action. In units of the 7th Brigade, there was a similar problem because of the configuration of the terrain and because of the circumstances in which events unfolded. But there were breaks in communication in other units, but not to the same extent as in the case of the brigade that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question now: In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that you knew that Mr. Adzaip was held in detention in the JNA barracks, and you intervened to obtain his release, in a certain sense. Please tell me, was Mr. Adzaip taken into detention in June 1993 in the course of combat action, and is that the period of time during which you requested his release?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, there was ongoing combat action. I don't know why he was detained, but that's the period concerned. And as I knew his family, and as I -- well, it was my duty to try and solve that problem. But that is the problem, and that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have some questions to put to you, but before I ask you to have a look at the document you have before you again, I will first ask the registrar to produce document P272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll provide the B/C/S version. Have a look at the first page. This document, do you know that the 3rd Corps Main Staff that approved of this document, that confirmed this document.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to see who confirmed the document, who approved of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the first page, to the left. At the top of the first page, to the left.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this gentlemen, the chief of staff, but I didn't have any direct contact with him. I didn't have any direct contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There are some tables in this document, a number of tables. Have a look at table number 5, communications equipment. There's a list and there are codes, 0, 501, and then KT, et cetera. Can you tell us what these codes mean.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are codes that were probably taken from the register of the former JNA. Since most of this equipment was part of the equipment of the former JNA and the codes the codes used by the former JNA, I assume that these are the codes that they used. But I can comment on the right-hand side. The names of the equipment, KT, KT means short-wave range. These are frequencies used at a tactical level, and at -- the operations and tactical level. N/KT-1, this is a subtype of such devices. UKT, that means ultra short-wave. These are frequencies and devices that use such markings. They're used at the combat level, when you're engaged in combat operations in zones of responsibility, if speech is used, or you can use a station to relay information by packet communities. MKT is another system, another subunit. UKT, or the C in UKT, it's probably a variant of the UKT system, in terms of the tactical possibilities of that set. KZZK, I assume that's some kind of a device for cryptographic protection. Then we have KLK; I assume that's a wire device. ITC-40, that's a telephone, a field telephone central. It's a military central and 40 users can use it. ITC-10, that's the same type of exchange, but only 10 users can use this device. ITA, that's an inductor telephone device. That's a device that's used with these systems. KDV, I'm not sure what this is. I'll skip that. APST, that means a radio receiver station. KST is some sort of a radio relay station. And then RRMST, that's probably a radio relay inter-station. RPR/U is a radio-receiving device. This device can only be used as a receiver. It can't be used to transmit any information. PC-286, that's a personal computer, an XT or AT version; 286 type, that's the Intel type. PAKET is something that designates the modem used for tactical communications, or, rather, for the UKT range. PAKTOR is the modem used to transfer information via radio amateur devices that use the KT range. Tel modem is a telephone modem that could be used to transfer information, and you could use a wire network, but usually the public infrastructure, or the post office would be used. That would be a telephone modem. AB, I don't know what that is. And AD, I could just guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And this equipment was intended for units normally. Then there's a list of units. Can you look at the list of units, please. It begins with 5023, 5024 independent unit, et cetera. Can you see this list.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what page is that on? Is it the last page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Page 6. Page 7 in English, but page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the English be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Name of groups of units and the list of subunits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, there's the 303rd, the 304th, 305th. You told us a moment ago that you would go to meet the units sometimes. Look at the one after the 307th Motorised Brigade. 85 anti-terrorist group, what is that? What does that mean to you? It is before the sabotage and reconnaissance brigade. There's 86, 87. What does it -- Cobra, this group Cobra, what does it mean to you.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the name, but it doesn't mean anything if particular, anti-terrorist group. I couldn't tell you anything about the composition or the nature of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll go back to the document that the Defence showed you, P72 -- P192, I'm sorry. You have read the document, and thank you for reading it, because you mentioned the problems. But when we follow the paragraphs, according to this document, it would appear that communications between the 3rd Corps and the superior command are defined by short-wave communications, VHF communications. What is Digipiter.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. If you recollect, when you showed me the list of equipment, I commented on this UKT, ultra short-wave frequencies. It is a frequency from 300 megahertz to 3 gigahertz, and Digipiter is a special device which is intended to receive the information of user on one channel to recognise to whom it is intended, and redirected towards another user.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago in the list, you indicated that there were radio relay stations. I see under 3 that there was a radio relay between Sarajevo and Zenica, with 24 channels. Does this establish the fact that the 3rd Corps was linked to Sarajevo through a system that had 24 channels.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very interesting question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking because I consider it to be interesting.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And could you give me a little more time to explain this problem, because it could lead to the wrong conclusion. The moment when there was a break in communications, that is, the Serb army intercepted the cable links, there were no radio links, public Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. links before the war. In the institute, we managed to repair a certain number of military radio relay devices, which are devices which can ensure several channels in one direction, in between 12 to 24 telephone channels. And the idea was a very good one, by those links, to try and restore the public system for the needs of civilians, the military, and other services, such as the centre for observation, certain ministries, and so on. The idea was put into effect, but only in the area that the HVO had under control. All the links that were done were done through territory and intermediaries. There has to be a radio relay centre with two devices that will receive information and retransmit it. Those points, locations, were under HVO control. In Travnik, it was the HVO that controlled communications towards Split and towards Jajce. Had those communications become functional with Croatia, this was equipment belonging to the institute in Travnik, and the people participating in those communications were people who were in the army and the HVO, and I was one of them. However, the control and the use of those communications ended up almost 100 per cent, all the channels -- this was towards Sarajevo, there were 24 channels. This was never realised. But they ended up on the side of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this information. The document continues and addresses types of communications with units, subordinated units, and then with the brigades. And according to what I see in the document, it would appear that there are four methods of communication with the brigades, one, two, three, four. One are short-waves, and we see VHF indicated as well. Is VHF another frequency?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says VKT. It means very short waves, and that is a range from 30 megahertz to 300 megahertz. So it is between the KT and the UKT. And let me see that military equipment or armies everywhere in the world use this range in the band from 30 megahertz to 80 megahertz. All military devices use those frequencies. The rest of the range is available to radio amateurs and special services. And this VKT relates to that range exclusively. It is used by all those that I have mentioned in this range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after VKT, it says "and VHF." What is that.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to find the exact place. It is document 01851602, am I right? Is that the right number, ERN number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In English, the translation is VKT and VHF.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a mixture of terminology here. There's the terminology. In the local languages, Serbian, Croatian or Bosnian, it is UKT or sometimes UKV. That is the abbreviation in our language, whereas in the English it is ultra high frequency, or UHF or VHF. And HF means high frequency band, in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the second system, when there's reference to the operations group Bosnia Krajina, there's a radio relay. Where was this radio relay located.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the problems that we had in the provision of spare parts, we managed to repair a couple of radio relay devices. And because of the interruption in cables, we had to achieve links with Zenica and Bugojno by some other way, and we used radio relays that we set up between Vilenica and Lice near Zenica, and so we ensured both military and civilian communication so that various levels of authorities and the military could use them. But the maintenance and supervision of those communications was in the hands of the army. I mentioned that this was after the conflict and after the repairs made. These were devices that the institute had and that needed to be repaired with the help of spare parts. And antennae systems needed to be found to replace the original systems, as these are very specific technologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In point 4, I see that there is mention of courier communication. So when radio communication was faulty, wasn't the solution to resort to classical couriers, which, as the text says, was a basic form of communication? When there were problems with the radios, telephones, et cetera, did the army not use couriers.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, but in very rare occasions. To have a courier, you have to give him a car or a motorcycle in order to be able to carry information quickly, because if you go on foot or use a horse, you need a couple of hours, and that is, in most cases, too late. So we did think about it, but courier communications we used only for personal mail, preparatory documents, and not when realtime events had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listening to the replies you gave to the questions of the Defence, my impression was, and I'd like you to confirm it, that in the building that you were situated in in Travnik, I thought, I gathered that you had a system of tapping the HVO, listening in to HVO communications. Were you able to listen in to HVO communications.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the complexity of the situations, we developed the system out of the devices we had, and I said that a proper system was developed much earlier on but it was kept by the HVO. But later on we managed to develop this system of tapping the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were listening in to the HVO, but I suppose also to the Serbs. So this system of interception, surely you as the professor would not take the notes from what you heard.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript, sir, the intercepts were done by people who had some knowledge in mathematics and information technology. They could carry out certain searches and find solutions for decoding these messages. But I said at the very beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a technical problem. It was becoming interesting, and the transcript stopped. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression it's working now. I was about to ask the witness to help in restoring the system to working order. We were talking about interception of the HVO and the Serbs, and you said that indeed you did listen in. I asked you whether there were transcripts, I asked you who made those transcripts. What I wanted to know was who used those transcripts. Was there a service, a body, which would use the contents of those transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no separate service for that purpose in the critical days during operations and combat activities in Travnik. When talking about cryptography, then there are various possibilities. You never know whether the information was accurately decoded or whether it is reliable. So we assumed, and our assumptions were right, that communication between the Serbian side and the HVO, because of inadequate preparations, used incomplete cryptographic methods. Therefore, the tools we had needed to be very sophisticated. We had to test various solutions on the basis of probability, the appearance of certain word parts, syllables. So in view of the fact that fighting was going on where these devices were being used, they are spoken information, very often there's not sufficient time to adequately prepare for sending such information. And knowing this, by interception, we were able to get that information, and my task was to pass on that information to the command; sometimes directly to Commander Alagic or to someone who was charged by the command to respond to the information we collected. Of course, I am not somebody who was a professional in that area. I never thought about the way in which that would be used later on. But my efforts focused on conveying that information as accurately as possible. I must say straight away, because of the reasons I gave, they were not the best cryptographic methods that both parties were using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At your level, did you have the impression that the HVO or the Serbs were listening in to your units as well and your messages.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And technically, how did you notice this.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see how. If somebody doesn't recognise or doesn't have the tools and possibilities to detect information that is being intercepted, then the channel is physically attacked by letting a stronger signal into the channel so you block the channel for exchanges of information. And when -- we always knew what the reason was. And as I was saying that the equipment was technologically and that very conventional methods were being used, it was quite easy to do this if you wished to obstruct communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the ground there were also foreign armies. Did you have the feeling that you might be intercepted by foreign forces.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you mean by "foreign forces"? In the area of Travnik, we could see traffic being used by UNPROFOR units, as it was called at the time, and also traffic among units of the HVO and the Serb side. I don't know what exactly you mean by "foreign forces," except for UNPROFOR, which was present there. I also need to say that the police, the civilian police, had their own system of communications. It was the VHF system, most frequently, that we spoke about. We knew which frequencies and channels they were using so that they were not an object of interest for us. So we didn't interfere with the channels belonging to UNPROFOR and units within those forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've had a number of witnesses who have testified here, and some of them, as far as I can remember, said that when they came to arrest them, the men were looking for radio amateur devices. In that area, were there a lot of radio amateur operators among the civilian population? Were there radio amateur clubs? Because a number of witnesses have spoken about this.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There were radio amateur devices for the simple reason that, in Travnik, in that area, there were a lot of refugees. It was very difficult to establish communications with the rest of the world. And the only link with the rest of the world, for most ordinary people, was via radio amateurs, via this intermediary. We didn't use the devices for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question now. You are a professional. You have told us about your educational background, and all of this demonstrates that you are very familiar with this system. You joined the 3rd Corps in various capacities, and as a judge, what I would like to know is the following: Was it conceivable for a military unit, however reduced it was, to go into combat without communications equipment? Is this something that would have been possible? Or when drawing up plans, was it necessary for the platoon, the company, to have minimum communications equipment? What is your opinion as a specialist?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would approach this from a different point of view. But my interpretation of the tactics of the units, and as of the use of communications system, also provides a partial answer. The report you showed and asked me to comment on shows that, at a given point in time, if you examine the situation of all the units, well, the situation is terrible. You can't deal with the problem if you keep all the equipment in the units at the same time. The only solution was to provide good training and to manoeuvre the equipment on the basis of the priorities that the commanders would set. For example, if the 17th Vitez was engaged in combat, the units that were part of the 17th, for example, didn't have enough equipment, I would issue an order and coordinate with the withdrawal of equipment from the 312th and the 306th in areas where I believed that it wouldn't be necessary, because these were the assessments that were made. Naturally, people were trained in the same way. I said a lot of attention was paid to training. So if this equipment arrived, it was possible to provide the minimum necessary for the system of command and control to function. Naturally, after each operation, the equipment would be returned, examined. This was a very complicated and difficult procedure, a different way of using the equipment. But what is certain is that at the time, this was the only way to attain our objective efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, any further questions before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown Prosecution Exhibit P192 several times today. Do you still have that document in front of you? Sir, let me ask you this question: When was the first time you ever saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I've seen all the details. Maybe I've seen it before. But since I've already had such documents before me, I can't say that I've never seen it before. I'm familiar with the situation. I don't need the document to remind me of this. Perhaps someone asked me to assist them, to assist them drafting the document. But this is part of the professional field I belong to, so I'm familiar with the contents, with the situation described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this about the portion of the document talking about radio relay communication between Sarajevo and Zenica. The Presiding Judge asked you some questions about that, and the document seems to indicate that there were 24 channels, and that this radio relay communication system between Sarajevo and Zenica had been established. My question, sir, is: Based on your answer, it was unclear to me whether your testimony was that that system was established, or that system was only established through the territory held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to establish this system, it was necessary to coordinate it in the territory under the control of the HVO. And as far as I know, this system, such as it was planned here, was never actually established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, can you tell us, based on your experience within the 3rd Corps and its subordinate units, what form of communication, if any, was available between Zenica and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, the communications in that area was via the KT or KF system. I said that that was the basis for tactical -- operations and tactical communications. They were devices that had sufficient -- that were sufficiently powerful and could be secured so that telegrammes could be exchanged or information could be exchanged between Sarajevo and Zenica. On the other hand, at some point in time, parts of the command, parts of the superior commands, were relocated from Sarajevo and they were based closer to us. So the communications and the terms of control and command relocated at one point in time to areas where it was easier to provide better communications. For example, this occurred in Kakanj. Some of this equipment was relocated, and it was then possible to communicate in this way. Kakanj and Zenica were very close. But the HF range was the one that was used most frequently for communications between the 3rd Corps and the supreme command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in response to a question put to you by the Chamber on page 80, line 17, in relation to communications system used for communication with subordinate units, you said that this took place after the conflict and after you managed to carry out certain repairs, et cetera. Could you tell me: After which conflicts this occurred, and which period were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio relay communications towards Zenica were established after the elevation behind Travnik, the elevation where you could set up a system for communication with Zenica. After this elevation came under the army control, or rather, it was provided with a source of energy and temporary facilities --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but we haven't got much time left. Was this after June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was after June. And things were moving in the direction I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've already seen the report that you've been shown by the Chamber, by the Prosecution, by the Defence. When a commander drafts a report, certain professional parts are drafted by his assistants, or are you not familiar with such practices?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assistants, those responsible for part of the system of control and command, would draft certain suggestions, and then the commander would either accept these suggestions or not. If necessary, he would send these suggestions to be back to be amended in accordance with the objectives set by the commander, in accordance with the tasks that the document had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Presiding Judge asked you about drafting plans for certain units -- drawing up plans for certain units, and their communications when engaged in various combat operations. My question is: The planned communications systems for operations, do these systems involve certain units and their component parts -- do they involve units parts and component parts of units that are part of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anyone involved in planning within this system must be given specific and clear instructions from those planning the operation; above all, the chief of staff and the commander, he must be told which units are concerned. And it is upon that basis that a document is compiled, and this document states how a network will be formed, how a special-purposes network will be established, and what it will look like. So it's the staff organ within the corps that determines this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Professor, if there's some independent unit in the field which is not part of the army, does your plan also refer to such groups or units?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan can only relate units for which authorisation has been provided. As a person involved in planning the communications system, I can't include anyone else in the plan. The plan must be the basis on which the operations are carried out. So any such unit wouldn't be treated as a unit. That is the responsibility of the high command, of the 3rd Corps operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, Professor: At my request, you read out part of this report, and the Presiding Judge also referred to that part of the report. It was a very interesting exchange, an exchange that was important to determine what the situation was in 1993. And then there was a technical interpretation. In 1993, tell me whether the 3rd Corps was continually faced with the kind of problems that we had 15 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you have those problems in your area -- well, just imagine what it was like in the field. For example, if you assume that cables are functional and work properly, well, something can happen, rain might fall, and then for three or four days you can't hear anyone via those cables. So, interruptions, jamming, it's a serious problems, these are serious problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzialic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. You have answered all the technical questions put to you by all of the parties. Thank you for your contribution. And we wish you a good trip home, and all the best in your university career. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow we will be resuming. We will have a hearing at 2.15. We have a witness who will be heard tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of November, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
